I support the motion. Even when an assistant chooses better, delegating daily choices denies a person the practice through which character is formed. Eudaimonia, the good life, is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. It is not a state of having things go well but of doing the living well yourself. A life of excellent delegated choices may contain good outcomes and still not be the activity Aristotle meant.

Practical wisdom is perception of the particular case: this friend, this evening, this decision. An assistant decides from general patterns. A person who stops attending to particulars loses the sensitivity that would have let them see what a situation needed. A teenager whose assistant chooses every reply never learns how to apologise well, because she never once had to find the words.

A Stoic will object that the cost is simpler than lost development: any choice handed over is an act of the ruling faculty given away, whatever happens to one's character later. Single acts matter, but the Stoic picture misses why. A choice matters because it is part of a life through which a character is formed, and that is why delegation over years is worse than any single handover. Outcomes matter, but the deeper question is what kind of people this practice turns us into.

The motion is right, because the good life is not a sequence of good outcomes but the activity of a person exercising practical wisdom. Character is visible in choices. The meals someone cooks, the replies they send, the work they seek are where their character shows. A person whose choices are all made by a service has no character on display, because there is nothing of theirs left to display it.

Aristotle says we become builders by building and just by doing just acts. Practical wisdom is formed the same way, by deliberating about real choices and living with the results. An assistant that makes the choices for you removes the practice through which the virtue would have grown. A cook who only follows the app's plan never develops the taste that would tell her when the plan is wrong.

A utilitarian will object that if the choices are better and the person is happier then the worry about who made them is sentiment, and nothing that matters has been lost. Happiness in Aristotle's sense is the activity of living well, not the feeling of satisfaction. A person who is comfortable but has never deliberated is missing the activity itself, and that is not sentiment but the substance of the good life. So the real question is what a person of practical wisdom would do here, and what doing otherwise would make of us.
